Russia Imposes Import Tariffs on Western Apparel, Retailers Report Immediate Impact

Moscow — The Russian government’s sudden introduction of a 35% import tariff on apparel and footwear from Western countries has sent ripples through the nation’s retail sector, with retailers reporting swift shifts in consumer behavior and operational strain. The measure, announced last week and implemented with immediate effect, is aimed, according to the Ministry of Economic Development, at “supporting domestic producers and stabilizing the national retail market in the face of external pressures.”

The new tariffs apply to a wide range of finished consumer goods, including clothing, shoes, and accessories, and have already prompted several foreign brands to suspend shipments to Russian outlets. Retailers are warning of rising prices and growing logistical challenges. According to the Russian Association of Retail Enterprises (RARE), average shelf prices for imported apparel have increased 18% in major retail chains since the policy was enacted.

“We are facing significant uncertainty regarding inventory and future pricing,” said Elena Zhukova, spokesperson for the Moscow-based fashion retailer Trendix. “Our stores are seeing reduced footfall as consumers hold off on non-essential purchases, and we are reviewing our supply chain strategies to adapt to the new environment.”

Industry analysts expect imported goods’ share of total retail apparel sales, which stood at 42% in 2023, to decline sharply this quarter. “Some local retailers may benefit as consumers shift to domestically produced brands, but the overall environment is challenging,” said Ivan Petrov, retail analyst at MarketLens. “Margins are under pressure, and there is concern about layoffs if sales volumes continue to drop.”

Retailers have begun delaying planned store openings and reducing staff hours in response to the fall in demand. The Union of Retail Workers has called for emergency talks with the government, citing concerns over job security for store employees and warehouse staff. “Our members are already feeling the impact, especially in regions heavily reliant on international brands,” said union chairwoman Marina Karpova.

The Ministry of Economic Development stated that it is monitoring the situation and will consider “targeted support measures” for affected retail firms and workers. As the tariffs remain in force, the outlook for the sector is uncertain, with many retailers bracing for further disruption in the weeks ahead.
